The first liquefied natural gas train under QatarEnergy's North Field East expansion project will be ready to start operation in November, two people aware of the company's plans said, offering Qatar a path to restoring some output lost to Iranian attacks.
Launching the train would be a major milestone for the world's largest LNG expansion project at a time when Qatar is still recovering from the damage caused by attacks on Ras Laffan, which wiped out 17 per cent of the country's LNG capacity.
LNG production from the train is expected to start in the first quarter of 2027, the people said.
QatarEnergy did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.
QatarEnergy Chief Executive Saad al-Kaabi said last month that the project was expected to begin production in the first half of 2027 despite the US-Israeli war against Iran and the resulting disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mehdy Touil — lead LNG specialist at Calypso Commodities, which develops AI solutions for LNG — said the next major step will be the introduction of feed gas followed by a gradual progression over several weeks towards the first LNG production.
"A sustained ramp-up will ultimately require the resumption of unrestricted transit through the Strait of Hormuz, but I expect QatarEnergy to have the first (North Field East) train ready regardless," he added.
Iranian attacks in March on Qatar's Ras Laffan facility damaged two LNG trains, repairs to which could take three years to complete, and one gas-to-liquids plant that will complete repairs in the first quarter of 2027.
Despite the damage, Qatar would be able to resume normal gas operations within weeks once the strait reopens, Kaabi said last month, adding that QatarEnergy is currently producing very little LNG.

Scientists at Oregon State University have introduced a novel category of light-responsive substances that can generate hydrogen from water, as reported by Hydrogen Central. The research, directed by Kyriakos Stylianou from the university's College of Science, focuses on a photocatalyst that produces hydrogen rapidly and efficiently without needing an extra costly metal catalyst.
These results might provide researchers with an additional instrument for cutting greenhouse gas emissions and tackling climate change. Hydrogen is commonly employed in fuel cells for vehicles and in ammonia production, metal refining and plastics manufacturing.
A catalyst hastens a chemical reaction without being permanently transformed, and a photocatalyst does the same when triggered by light. Upon absorbing light, the material attains a higher energy state and can employ that energy to accelerate reactions, Stylianou explained.
The study examines metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs, which are crystalline porous substances constructed from positively charged metal ions encircled by organic linker molecules. Their minuscule pores and modifiable structures enable scientists to adjust properties for various purposes. Stylianou noted that millions of distinct MOF structures are theoretically feasible, with chemists having already synthesized close to 100,000 MOFs and forecast the properties of approximately 500,000 additional ones.
The group zeroed in on a MOF named BVR-19, which possesses an uncommon sulfide-to-sulfide bond that briefly ruptures upon light exposure, generating highly reactive sulfur species. Stylianou stated that the organic part performs the crucial function. Instead of depending primarily on metal atoms, the substance utilizes its sulfur-bearing organic building blocks to harvest light energy and transfer electrons toward hydrogen generation. He characterized the strategy as an alternative perspective on how such materials ought to be engineered.
This design means BVR-19 needs no extra expensive metal catalyst, potentially streamlining forthcoming light-powered hydrogen systems. The material also assembles spontaneously in aqueous solutions at ambient temperature, reducing the energy required to create it.
Using a catalyst to split water can be more environmentally friendly than the prevailing industrial technique, methane-steam reforming, which relies on natural gas and emits carbon dioxide during hydrogen production. Current water-splitting approaches frequently depend on electrocatalysis, whose ecological advantage hinges on the origin of the electricity. To be both sustainable and economically viable, that electricity must derive from inexpensive renewable sources.
Expense continues to be an obstacle. Methane-steam reforming produces hydrogen at roughly $1.50 per kilogram, or $0.68 per pound, whereas green hydrogen costs about $5 per kilogram, or $2.27 per pound.
Stylianou, who heads Oregon State's Materials Discovery Laboratory, remarked that the research provides a template for engineering materials that lower the cost of green hydrogen. By altering the metal while leaving the remainder of the material largely unchanged, his group discovered why certain versions of the MOF perform far better than others. Those results supply fresh design guidelines for developing more potent materials for solar fuel generation.

Long-term offtake agreements can connect upstream natural gas resources with international LNG markets. For ConocoPhillips, the agreement adds contracted LNG volumes to a portfolio that includes previously secured arrangements.

The facility is designed to produce LNG for international markets, connecting U.S. natural gas supplies with overseas customers. Gulf Coast infrastructure provides access to established pipeline networks, export terminals, shipping routes, and natural gas production regions.

The combination of U.S. and Qatari projects gives the LNG portfolio exposure to different production regions, infrastructure systems, and international customer markets.
Willow and Permian Operations

North Sea Asset Review

The North Sea has a long history of oil and natural gas production, with mature infrastructure and established offshore supply chains. Portfolio changes in the region form part of broader asset-management activity as ConocoPhillips evaluates the composition of its international operations.
The review occurs alongside LNG expansion, creating two distinct strands within the companys portfolio: development of long-duration LNG activities and changes to selected upstream assets.
LNG Marketing and Global Gas Markets
LNG marketing represents an expanding component of ConocoPhillips business profile. Long-term supply agreements can establish links between production assets, LNG facilities, shipping networks, and international buyers.
Global LNG markets connect natural gas producers with customers across Europe, Asia, and other importing regions. Demand is influenced by electricity generation, industrial consumption, heating, infrastructure development, and changes in regional energy systems.
For ConocoPhillips, the Venture Global agreement adds contracted LNG supply while Port Arthur and Qatar projects provide additional exposure to LNG production and international markets.
ConocoPhillips Within the S&P 500
ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP) ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP) remains closely associated with the energy sector through its upstream oil and natural gas operations, while LNG development adds an increasingly prominent international gas component.

The Venture Global agreement adds another layer to that business profile, connecting long-term LNG supply with existing developments at Port Arthur and in Qatar. The resulting portfolio combines traditional upstream production with international LNG activities and ongoing asset restructuring.

articles.title: POSCO Doubles Down on Argentina Lithium With New 23,000-Ton Plant - ChemAnalyst

articles.full_text:
Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	POSCO Holdings has completed the upstream process of its second brine-based lithium plant in Argentina, marking a major expansion of its lithium supply chain and strengthening its position in the global battery materials market.
	The company held a completion ceremony on October 6 near the Hombre Muerto salt lake, located roughly 4,000 meters above sea level. The event brought together senior officials from South Korea and Argentina, including POSCO Group Chairman Chang In-hwa, Argentine Presidential Chief of Staff Karina Milei, Salta Governor Gustavo Saenz and South Korean Ambassador to Argentina Lee Jong-hwa.
	The second plant represents an investment of approximately $954 million and has an annual production capacity of 23,000 tons of lithium carbonate. Together with POSCO's first operating plant, which has a capacity of 25,000 tons annually, the company's lithium carbonate production capacity in Argentina will rise to approximately 48,000 tons per year.
	The lithium carbonate produced in Argentina will be transported to POSCO's downstream processing facilities at the Yulchon Industrial Complex in South Korea. The downstream facility is scheduled for completion next year and will convert the material into battery-grade lithium hydroxide.
	Once the downstream operation is integrated with existing production, POSCO Group expects to establish an independently controlled brine-based lithium hydroxide supply chain with total capacity of approximately 50,000 tons per year.
	The development represents the culmination of an eight-year journey since POSCO acquired local salt-lake mining rights in 2018. Chairman Chang has been closely involved in the project since his tenure leading the group's new business office in 2014, when he visited Argentina to identify suitable lithium resources.
	The latest expansion also signals that POSCO is preparing for another significant production increase. On October 6, the company signed memoranda of understanding with the provincial governments of Salta and Catamarca to advance plans for its third and fourth lithium plants.
	Each proposed facility is expected to have an annual production capacity of 25,000 tons, potentially adding another 50,000 tons of capacity. POSCO is targeting a total brine lithium production system of 100,000 tons annually by 2033.
	The company expects growing demand from energy storage systems and lithium iron phosphate batteries to support future lithium consumption, particularly as AI data centers accelerate electricity demand and the deployment of grid-scale storage.
	The expansion could give POSCO greater control over upstream resources and reduce its exposure to external lithium suppliers. For battery manufacturers, additional integrated production could also improve long-term availability of battery-grade lithium hydroxide.
	Product and Chemical Commodity Price Impact
POSCO's expanded Argentine brine operation is expected to increase the availability of lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide, strengthening its vertically integrated battery-materials supply chain. In the near term, the additional 23,000 tons of lithium carbonate capacity could add supply to an already competitive lithium market, limiting upside pressure on lithium carbonate prices. Increased downstream conversion into battery-grade lithium hydroxide could similarly weigh on hydroxide premiums if demand growth fails to absorb new volumes. However, POSCO's planned third and fourth plants signal stronger long-term demand expectations from ESS and LFP batteries. Therefore, lithium prices may remain under pressure initially but could find support as battery and storage demand accelerates.

articles.title: National Lab partnership helps launch U.S. lithium supply chain - Newswise

Newswise — With support from U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratories, including Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), Texas-based company Element3 has launched the first domestic lithium mining project in 50 years. This achievement is likely to have a big impact, turning the United States from a net importer of lithium to a country well on the path to greater energy independence, national security, and economic strength.
The milestone, in February 2026, came less than a year after DOE launched the Minerals to Materials Supply Chain Research Facility, or METALLIC, in April 2025. The facility builds on DOE demonstration testbeds to speed technologies that strengthen the nation’s supply chain of minerals critical to the technology, transportation, and defense industries. It provides experts and tools to de-risk development of these critical minerals technologies.
National Labs help partners strengthen their domestic supply chains
Led by the National Energy Technology Laboratory, nine DOE National Labs operate four METALLIC centers. The centers focus on improving feedstock purity, extracting and separating minerals using energy-saving methods, refining salts and oxides into metals, and developing alloys for advanced manufacturing.
Companies and universities work with the national labs to test and validate technologies as they progress from the lab scale to pilot plants. The centers connect technology developers, suppliers, and users to strengthen U.S. supply chains for critical minerals including rare earth elements, platinum group metals, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, gallium, and germanium.
“We want to optimize material processing methods, reduce environmental impact and recover more value from materials,” said ORNL’s Parans Paranthaman, who leads METALLIC’s Extractions and Separations Center.
The center is co-led by Argonne and Idaho national laboratories. Partners include Ames, Lawrence Berkeley, Lawrence Livermore and Pacific Northwest national laboratories and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The team works to expand and diversify mineral sources and test new extraction methods, including chemistry guided by Super Intelligence (SI).
ORNL’s METALLIC team provides diverse expertise. Chemists and chemical engineers including Ramesh Bhave, Barbara Evans, Syed Islam, Jayanthi Kumar, Katie Johnson, Bruce Moyer, Pasindu Samaraweera, Saurabh Prakash Pethe, Shailesh Dangwal and Donga Kang provide expertise in membranes, solvent extraction and absorption methods to find new ways to extract lithium, gallium, germanium, and rare earths. Physical chemist Craig Bridges designs SI-enabled autonomous labs for process optimization. Nanomaterials experts Rigoberto Advincula and Ilia Ivanov use ORNL’s Center for Nanophase Materials Sciences to probe characteristics of columns packed with sorbents that separate lithium from brine. Other ORNL staff members, interns, graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers contribute as well.
“We want industry partners to come and use the national lab capabilities and test their systems,” Paranthaman said.
New lithium supply strengthens U.S. security, economy
Element3 focuses on extracting lithium from wastewater generated during oil production in the Permian Basin. Back in 2024, the company had licensed technology that was batteries">developed by Paranthaman’s ORNL team. The innovation won an R&D 100 Award that year. Recently, this team won the 2026 Excellence in Technology Transfer Award from the Federal Laboratory Consortium.
The process selectively extracts lithium from produced water, which is derived from oil and gas extraction. This wastewater contains lithium. Leveraging ORNL’s technology, the company recovers lithium chloride and converts it to battery-grade lithium carbonate powder.
“The feedstock contains all kinds of elements, so you need to selectively extract the element of interest with high efficiency and low cost as you scale up,” Paranthaman said.
On Feb. 6, Paranthaman attended a ribbon-cutting to celebrate the opening of Element3’s lithium extraction plant in Midland, Texas. The plant extracts lithium chloride from produced water and converts it to lithium carbonate.
Element3 has now deployed its first commercial lithium extraction plant in the Permian Basin using ORNL technology. This completes the scaling of the technology from the laboratory to a commercial operation. It marks the first new lithium mining project to market in the United States since the late 1960s.
Element3’s lithium carbonate facility can produce 3,000 tons of lithium per year — nearly half of the current U.S. production. Lithium is used in some vehicle batteries and smartphones and could help provide grid-scale energy storage.
For decades, much lithium processing has occurred overseas, where labor is cheaper and environmental protections are less stringent. This facility signals a shift toward U.S.-based production.
“We can produce our own starting materials, like for battery manufacturing for example,” Paranthaman said. “You need lithium hydroxide or lithium carbonate, and we are producing those chemicals at the Texas site. We are doing the separation to produce our own lithium. This is a domestic supply chain.”
“Thanks to the support of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, we have been able to leverage existing technology to solve our challenges and accelerate our path to market,” said Element3 chief executive officer Hood Whitson.
“The success of Element3 is what METALLIC’s innovation ecosystem aims to emulate with keystone companies,” Paranthaman said.
The Critical Materials Innovation Hub and Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office, which are part of an Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation effort, supported the initial development of ORNL work.
UT-Battelle manages ORNL for DOE’s Office of Science, the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States. The Office of Science is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time. For more information, please visit energy.gov/science. — Dawn Levy

Highlights
- Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE:FCX) Basic Materials Freeport-McMoran Copper & Gold Inc (NYSE:FCX) 71.86 USD -0.700 0.965% Last Updated at: 2026-10-07T20:20:00Z is in focus as copper stays firm on electrification and data-center demand.

Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE:FCX) Basic Materials Freeport-McMoran Copper & Gold Inc (NYSE:FCX) 71.86 USD -0.700 0.965% Last Updated at: 2026-10-07T20:20:00Z is back in the spotlight on Wednesday as copper continues to command attention across commodity desks, with the producer's recent quarterly report still shaping conversation about how the red metal is faring against a backdrop of electrification and data-center construction. The company has said it is positioned exceptionally well as the world electrifies, and that message has resonated through a market eager for supply-constrained materials.
Copper has spent much of the year firm, supported by tight concentrate availability, steady demand from grid builders and a growing appetite from technology companies erecting power-hungry facilities. Freeport sits near the center of that story as one of the largest publicly traded copper producers in the world, with operations spanning North America, South America and Indonesia.
The latest session has also been shaped by a broader tone of firm metal prices. Gold remains near record highs and crude has been firming toward higher levels, a combination that keeps miners in the headlines while reminding the industry that energy costs remain a moving part of every operating budget.
What the Latest Quarter Revealed
Freeport's second-quarter report showed earnings rising from the year-earlier period even as revenue declined modestly, a mix that reflects the interplay between realized prices, sales volumes and unit costs. Revenue still came in ahead of what the market had expected, which helped reinforce the view that the company is executing steadily through a complicated operating year.
Management described the business as entering a period of growth in its Americas operations, pointing to leach projects and mining-plan improvements designed to extract more metal from existing ore bodies. That emphasis on squeezing additional output from established assets is a hallmark of how large copper producers are responding to the scarcity of new discoveries.
Electrification Keeps Demand Structurally Firm
Copper's role in the energy transition is difficult to overstate. Electric vehicles use far more of the metal than conventional cars, charging networks require extensive cabling, and renewable generation from wind and solar depends on copper-rich transmission and storage infrastructure. Each of those categories has been expanding even as the federal electric vehicle incentive expiration reshapes near-term demand in North America.
The expiration of federal incentives has created uneven conditions for automakers, yet the global picture remains supportive for copper because electrification is not confined to one country or one product. Grid modernization programs in Europe and Asia, together with utility upgrades across the United States, continue to absorb large volumes of refined metal.
Data Centers and the Artificial Intelligence Build-Out
One of the more striking themes this year has been the influence of artificial intelligence infrastructure on base metals. A strong semiconductor rally and heavy chip capital spending have been accompanied by a wave of data-center construction, and every new facility demands copper for power distribution, busbars, cooling systems and backup generation.
The connection between chips and copper is indirect but meaningful. Facilities packed with accelerators draw enormous amounts of electricity, which in turn requires new substations, longer transmission lines and upgraded local grids. Utilities and industrial contractors have been lifted by that wave, and copper suppliers are increasingly viewed as upstream beneficiaries.
Sector Context Across Metals and Mining
The wider group of Metals and Mining Stocks has been supported by a convergence of favorable conditions: strong precious-metal prices, firm industrial metals and persistent talk of supply constraints. Large miners have used the stronger tape to advance growth projects that were deferred during softer periods.
Within that group, copper has become the focal point. The metal's mix of cyclical and structural demand drivers has made it the preferred shorthand for the electrification theme, and equities tied to it have often moved in step with swings in copper futures and shifts in sentiment about global manufacturing.
Market Environment and Equity Sentiment
The broader equity backdrop has been constructive, with technology and industrial shares leading advances and cyclical sectors participating selectively. Freeport is a component of the S&P 500, and its performance often serves as a barometer for market appetite toward commodity-sensitive parts of the equity universe.
Mining equities have a tendency to react quickly to changes in copper futures, to dollar movements and to shifts in Chinese economic data. A softer dollar generally supports dollar-priced commodities, while indications of stronger Chinese manufacturing tend to lift sentiment around base metals.
Broader Market Relevance of Freeport's Story
Freeport's progress is relevant well beyond mining circles. Copper serves as an economic bellwether, and the movement of the metal is often read as a signal about the health of global industry, construction and technology spending. For that reason, developments at a major producer tend to attract attention from macro-oriented market participants.
The company also illustrates how traditional industries are being repriced by new technology cycles. Artificial intelligence, electrified transport and grid renewal have all changed the way capital markets think about basic materials, shifting copper from a purely cyclical commodity toward one with a stronger structural component.

- Evolve Royalties Ltd. recorded a 2.46% decline on October 6, 2026, reflecting moderate Secondary Market distribution, selective institutional risk appetite, and multiple sensitivity across Canadian-listed base metals Royalty and streaming equities.
- The company centers its commercial framework on acquiring, creating, and managing high-margin royalties and streams focused primarily on strategic copper and critical base metal deposits across established Mining jurisdictions in Canada and the Americas.
- Operating performance remains structurally dependent on third-party mine operator execution, where partner feasibility studies, mine construction schedules, and regional environmental permitting timelines govern attributable Volume deliverability.

- Investor sentiment remains highly sensitive to operator drilling disclosures, partner financing milestones, strategic transaction integration, and broader industrial metals market volatility.
Introduction
Evolve Royalties Ltd. (CN:EVR) is a Canadian resource royalty and streaming corporation listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange. Headquartered in Vancouver, British Columbia, the organization operates with a commercial mandate to apply the royalty and streaming Business model to strategic copper and critical minerals Assets required for global electrification and the energy transition. Operating with a capital-light business architecture, the enterprise provides non-dilutive development financing to mining operators in exchange for top-line Revenue participation, net smelter return (NSR) royalties, and contractual metal delivery streams. Through this structure, the corporation secures economic participation in resource expansions and long-term commodity upside without assuming direct Liability for day-to-day mine operating costs, sustaining capital expenditures, or environmental reclamation burdens. Consequently, the organization's corporate velocity, Cash Flow profile, and public market Equity valuation depend directly on partner operator throughput, metallurgical recovery rates, realized physical copper and byproduct metal pricing, and technical milestone execution across pre-production royalty assets.
The stock's 2.46% decline on October 6, 2026 indicates renewed near-term selling pressure around an emerging royalty vehicle whose valuation remains sensitive to portfolio execution, partner operating delivery schedules, and broader equity market sentiment. While Evolve Royalties has actively expanded its asset base and advanced strategic transactions across high-quality copper targets, investors may remain cautious until expanding portfolio assets consistently translate into predictable, multi-asset quarterly cash flows. With no specific operational disruption or negative corporate catalyst established on the day of the move, the decline appears consistent with orderly profit-taking and broader institutional portfolio Rebalancing across small- and mid-cap resource platforms.
The overarching industrial metals backdrop presents distinct structural opportunities alongside persistent cyclical friction. Although long-term fundamentals for copper remain supported by global electrification, clean-energy grid expansion, and persistent primary Supply constraints, junior and intermediate resource equities frequently experience Collateral selling during broader market consolidations. Elevating benchmark borrowing costs, inflationary pressures across heavy industrial mine construction, and selective institutional capital access have heightened investor scrutiny, prompting Market Participants to demand demonstrated portfolio cash generation and disciplined capital allocation before assigning sustained valuation premiums to emerging base metals royalty platforms.
Key Reasons Behind Decline
Weak investor sentiment: The recent red close suggests that secondary market participants remain cautious toward junior and emerging resource royalty vehicles. When broader macroeconomic and financial conditions turn volatile, institutional portfolio managers routinely reduce exposure to smaller royalty platforms where multi-asset revenue Diversification remains an ongoing strategic transition, generating sustained downward pressure on share prices.
Sector weakness across base and industrial metals equities: Despite constructive multi-year commodity fundamentals for copper, resource equities frequently experience collateral selling during broader market consolidations. When financial market sentiment turns risk-averse, base metals equities face institutional profit-taking, dampening baseline valuation multiples across the entire peer group.
Operational challenges and partner execution dynamics: Because royalty corporations do not manage underlying mine infrastructure, revenue realization depends entirely on third-party mining operators executing according to schedule. When partner operators encounter localized engineering adjustments, mill throughput delays, or permitting review extensions at advanced development projects, royalty delivery timelines experience unanticipated deferrals.
Poor execution and timeline friction: Delays by operating partners in bringing newly constructed mining assets into commercial extraction or extended intervals between technical engineering updates can test market patience, prompting tactical profit-taking following periods of share appreciation.
The demand outlook for industrial commodities: Cautious global Manufacturing indicators and regional construction slowdowns have prompted periodic reassessments of near-term copper consumption. Market participants remain guarded regarding the cadence of international industrial demand and how supply-demand balances will influence spot base metal realization pricing.
Macroeconomic pressure and Interest Rate dynamics: Elevated benchmark borrowing costs and sovereign bond yields create competitive yield hurdles against non-operating, yield-oriented resource platforms, keeping institutional capital cautious.
Funding pressure and capital allocation discipline: Sourcing accretive, high-quality copper royalty and streaming transactions in a competitive landscape requires substantial capital liquidity. In an environment characterized by elevated capital costs, bidding for premium assets against established streaming peers demands disciplined balance sheet management.
Commodity volatility: Fluctuations in benchmark spot and forward copper prices directly govern modeled net asset values and future cash flow projections across the portfolio. Even though royalty agreements insulate companies from direct site-level cost inflation, public market multiples remain highly sensitive to revisions in underlying commodity price forecasts.

articles.title: Mexico’s Strategic Position on Latin America’s Hydrogen Map - Mexico Business News
articles.summary: Mexico’s Strategic Position on Latin America’s Hydrogen Map  Mexico Business News
articles.full_text:
Mexico is positioned to play a leading role in Latin America’s hydrogen sector, thanks to its exceptional renewable resources, its strategic geographic location, and its preferential access to the North American market through the USMCA trade agreement. With 31 clean hydrogen projects under development, representing an investment of approximately US$23 billion, the country is already demonstrating decisive momentum in building its hydrogen industry.
Mexico’s membership in the global solar belt provides it with among the highest solar irradiation levels in the world, forming the foundation for competitive renewable hydrogen production. The country possesses significant solar, wind, and geothermal capacity, circumstances that can drive renewable hydrogen production at scale.
This abundant renewable resource base translates directly into cost advantages. The Hydrogen Council’s Hydrogen Insights document mentions that Mexico could achieve up to 63% lower renewable hydrogen production costs compared to other countries, a competitive edge that stems primarily from its superior renewable resource quality.
Geographic and Trade Advantages
Mexico’s geographic position offers dual strategic benefits for hydrogen development and export. The southern region of the country serves as a continental nexus, maintaining strong commercial and business ties with both Central and South American nations despite Mexico’s classification as part of North America. Simultaneously, Mexico’s access to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans enables hydrogen exports to diverse global markets, from Asia-Pacific economies to European buyers.
The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) provides Mexico with preferential access to the world’s largest consumer market. This trade framework allows Mexico to export clean hydrogen to the United States and Canada under favorable commercial conditions while also positioning the country as a manufacturing hub for hydrogen-related equipment. Mexican industry could produce electrolyzers, turbines, fuel cells, hydrogen vehicles, and compressors for export to North American markets, leveraging existing industrial infrastructure established under the trade agreement.
Current Industry Momentum
Mexico’s clean hydrogen industry is advancing with notable determination. The country currently has 31 projects in different stages of development with investments totaling around US$23 billion. These projects will produce green and turquoise hydrogen, green ammonia, methanol, and geological or white hydrogen through Pemex initiatives.
Two green hydrogen production plants are already operational in the states of Queretaro and San Luis Potosí, demonstrating that Mexico has moved beyond the planning phase into actual production. This year, Mexico was selected to lead the Latin American Hydrogen Alliance, which brings together hydrogen associations from Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Peru, Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile, and Mexico. This leadership position enables Mexico to articulate efforts and align objectives for homogeneous development of the renewable hydrogen industry across Latin America.
Recent Policy Developments
In a significant policy development announced in late September 2026, Mexico’s Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) incorporated green hydrogen into its 2026-2030 Development and Strengthening Program. The program includes a 20MW green hydrogen project under mixed investment schemes for the expansion period. While modest in capacity, this inclusion marks an important step by formally recognizing hydrogen within CFE’s technology portfolio for national electric system expansion and diversification.
The CFE program contemplates 52 expansion projects with a capacity of 18,597MW and an investment of MX$467 billion (US$26 billion). The plan foresees the installation of 15,203MW of renewable capacity, including solar photovoltaic, wind, solar thermal, and geothermal technologies, among others. This incorporation represents a substantive part of the new capacity planned for the period and reflects the growing role of clean energy within CFE’s expansion strategy.
The participation of renewable energy in CFE’s generation is projected to rise, moving from 21% in 2025 to 34% in 2030. This evolution forms part of a strategy oriented toward diversifying the energy matrix and increasing the participation of technologies with lower carbon footprints.
Hydrocarbon Sector Planning
The Hydrocarbon Sector Development Plan (PLADESHi) incorporates energy transition and decarbonization as part of the sector’s transformation strategy. Within this framework, the document identifies green hydrogen as an element with potential for industrial decarbonization through its production via electrolysis powered by renewable energy. According to the plan, PEMEX will be able to evaluate various technological alternatives to optimize costs and resource availability, with potential applications in internal processes, renewable fuel production, and CO₂ capture and utilization schemes.
The plan also contemplates sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) development through a value chain that includes installing a biorefinery to transform raw materials such as ethanol into bio-jet fuel. The objective is to reach a target participation of 5% SAF in national aviation fuel consumption by 2030, contributing to the diversification of PEMEX’s revenues and the decarbonization of the aeronautical sector. Both green hydrogen and SAF are framed within a broader strategy oriented toward incorporating clean energy and technologies with lower environmental impact into hydrocarbon value chains.
Infrastructure Considerations
The growing incorporation of renewable generation also presents new challenges for National Electric System operation and reliability. In this context, the program highlights the importance of strengthening electrical infrastructure and incorporating technologies that enable reliable integration of new capacity.
Energy storage acquires relevance in this process as a complementary technology to manage the variability of sources such as solar and wind, as well as to contribute to system stability and flexibility. While the program does not establish specific energy storage capacity, its integration forms part of the technological context associated with incorporating new renewable capacity and strengthening system reliability.
An important expansion of transmission infrastructure joins this effort. For the 2026-2030 period, 175 projects and 7,545 additional kilometers of transmission lines are contemplated, with investments aimed at modernizing and strengthening electrical networks. This infrastructure will be fundamental for accompanying renewable generation growth and facilitating its integration into the national system, particularly given a matrix with an increasingly larger participation of variable sources.
Regional Leadership and Next Steps
Mexico’s hydrogen ambitions extend beyond national development to regional coordination. By leading the Latin American Hydrogen Alliance, Mexico can articulate efforts and align objectives for homogeneous development of the renewable hydrogen industry across Latin America, further cementing its role as a regional hub.
For Mexico to fully realize its potential as Latin America’s hydrogen leader, continued policy development, regulatory clarity, and sustained investment in both production capacity and enabling infrastructure will be essential. The foundation is in place: exceptional renewable resources, strategic geography, trade advantages, growing project pipelines, and emerging policy recognition. The trajectory now points toward Mexico becoming not just a regional participant but a defining force in Latin America’s hydrogen economy.

Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	Sigma Lithium has resumed mining and processing operations at its Grota do Cirilo lithium project in Brazil after a federal appeals court upheld the company’s environmental licences, removing a major legal hurdle that had disrupted production.
	The company said the appeals court overturned an emergency order issued last month by a federal judge in Teofilo Otoni, which had temporarily suspended the licences covering its operations. The latest ruling allows Sigma Lithium to fully restart mining and processing activities at the project.
	The legal dispute stems from a lawsuit filed by Ngolo, an association representing local Quilombola communities. Sigma said its mining activities are located outside the newly claimed community perimeter and maintained that its environmental licences were granted in accordance with applicable regulations.
	With operations restored, Sigma Lithium is reaffirming its target of reaching an annualized production rate of 330,000 tonnes of lithium oxide concentrate by the end of 2027. The company said it does not require additional mining or processing capacity to achieve that target, citing available capacity at its South Pit, existing processing plant, and recycling and reprocessing circuits installed as part of a 2024 upgrade.
	The processing facility has demonstrated significant throughput capability. Sigma said the plant previously produced more than 950 tonnes of lithium concentrate per day, with output exceeding 1,000 tonnes on several days following the upgrade.
	The company is also preparing for further expansion. Sigma plans to restart its second expansion phase in 2027, which could increase annual production capacity to approximately 580,000 tonnes. A subsequent third phase is planned to raise capacity further to around 830,000 tonnes annually.
	The resumption is particularly significant for the battery-materials supply chain because lithium concentrate produced at Grota do Cirilo is used in the manufacture of lithium-based battery materials. A sustained recovery in production could improve the availability of spodumene concentrate and strengthen supply visibility for downstream lithium processors.
	However, the project's expansion remains subject to operational execution and the outcome of ongoing community-related legal and regulatory issues. For lithium consumers and battery-material manufacturers, the immediate restart removes a supply disruption risk, while the planned capacity additions could have a more pronounced effect on market balances over the longer term.
	Product and Chemical Commodity Price Impact
The restart of Grota do Cirilo is bearish-to-neutral for lithium prices in the near term, as restored production reduces concerns over concentrate availability and strengthens expectations of additional supply. Higher operating rates could increase spodumene concentrate availability for converters, potentially limiting upward price momentum in lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide markets if demand does not accelerate simultaneously. The planned expansion toward 580,000 tonnes and eventually 830,000 tonnes of annual capacity could create a larger supply cushion over the medium term. For ChemAnalyst-tracked battery chemicals, the development may therefore pressure lithium feedstock costs, although EV demand, Chinese conversion rates, inventories and project execution will remain key price drivers.

articles.title: UK Urged to Turn Hydrogen Ambition Into Industrial Growth on World Hydrogen Day - AZoCleantech
articles.summary: UK Urged to Turn Hydrogen Ambition Into Industrial Growth on World Hydrogen Day  AZoCleantech
articles.full_text:
The UK has an opportunity to turn its growing hydrogen industry into an engine for regional growth, industrial renewal and energy security - but the time for delivery is now.
That is the message from the Hydrogen Energy Association (HEA) on World Hydrogen Day, as it calls for continued action to give businesses and investors the certainty needed to scale up projects, manufacturing and supply chains across the country.
The Association, which represents close to 100 organizations across the full hydrogen value chain, says Britain already has many of the ingredients needed to build a successful hydrogen economy - industrial expertise, established engineering and manufacturing capability, emerging projects and a workforce with highly transferable skills.
But it says the next phase must be about converting that potential into commercial deployment.
Dr Emma Guthrie, Chief Executive of the Hydrogen Energy Association, said: “World Hydrogen Day should be about more than celebrating the potential of hydrogen. It should be about asking what we need to do now to turn that potential into economic value for the UK.
“The opportunity is significant. Hydrogen can support skilled jobs in our industrial regions, strengthen UK supply chains, attract private investment, improve energy resilience and help businesses decarbonize.
“Those outcomes closely align with the country's wider ambitions for economic growth, industrial renewal and energy security. The hydrogen sector is ready to play its part.
“But opportunity alone does not create investment. Businesses need confidence, and confidence comes from clarity, consistency and a clear long-term direction.
“Now is the moment to maximize hydrogen's industrial and regional growth opportunity.”
The HEA is calling for clear and timely delivery of the policy framework for hydrogen, including progress through the Hydrogen Allocation Rounds, a clear long-term strategic direction for the sector and measures that maximize the value of public support by helping British supply chains grow alongside hydrogen deployment.
The call comes as hydrogen activity becomes increasingly concentrated in some of the UK's traditional industrial heartlands, including the North East, North West, South Wales and Scotland - creating the potential to support skilled employment and new investment in regions central to the UK's industrial future.
The scale of the opportunity was highlighted in the HEA's 2026 State of the Hydrogen Nation report.
Businesses surveyed for the report indicated that the sector could support around 4,000 direct jobs by 2030 under the current trajectory, compared with around 17,000 under an improved policy landscape - more than four times as many.
The report also identified Scotland, North East England and North West England as the three most attractive UK regions for hydrogen investment, underlining the potential relationship between hydrogen deployment and regional industrial growth.
There is a wider supply-chain prize too.
Analysis highlighted by the HEA from the Hydrogen Innovation Initiative suggests that securing a 10% share of the global hydrogen technology market could contribute £46 billion a year to the UK economy by 2050 and support 410,000 jobs.
The HEA argues that the economic case should not be considered solely through the cost of individual hydrogen projects.
Hydrogen production, storage and use can form part of a wider energy system capable of managing renewable intermittency, reducing curtailment, strengthening energy security and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. The Association says future decisions should therefore take account of hydrogen's potential impact on whole-system energy costs, alongside its industrial and decarbonization benefits.
Momentum is already building.
Projects across the country are moving from development towards commercial delivery, while the Government's second Hydrogen Allocation Round shortlisted 27 electrolytic hydrogen projects across England, Scotland and Wales.
HEA members are also demonstrating the breadth of the emerging market, from hydrogen production and storage to transport, industrial applications, infrastructure and new production pathways.
Dr Guthrie added: “We are no longer talking about a hypothetical industry. Businesses are investing, projects are being developed and British companies are building expertise that can compete internationally.
“The question is how quickly and how successfully we turn that momentum into a scaled UK market.
“Public support should do more than enable individual projects. Used strategically, programs such as the Hydrogen Allocation Rounds can help stimulate domestic manufacturing, strengthen supply chains and ensure that more of the economic and social value created by hydrogen stays here in Britain.
“That requires Government and industry to continue working closely together. We ultimately want the same things - economic growth, greater energy resilience, thriving industrial regions and a successful transition to a lower-carbon economy.
“On World Hydrogen Day, our message is simple: the opportunity is here. Now is the time to turn ambition into delivery.”
The HEA has been working with parliamentarians and Government to build understanding of the sector and the policy conditions needed for it to grow.
Ahead of the summer recess, its parliamentary campaign resulted in 34 written parliamentary questions being tabled on hydrogen-related issues, helping bring questions around investment, deployment and policy certainty directly into Parliament.
The Association will continue engaging with ministers, parliamentarians and industry to support the development of a competitive UK hydrogen economy.

articles.title: How St. Augustine Gold and Copper Ltd. (TSX: SAU) Is Lining Up Funding for the Kingking Copper-Gold Project - kalkine.ca
articles.summary: How St. Augustine Gold and Copper Ltd. (TSX: SAU) Is Lining Up Funding for the Kingking Copper-Gold Project  kalkine.ca
articles.full_text:
Funding is now the central question
How is St. Augustine Gold and Copper Ltd. (TSX:SAU) trying to move its Kingking copper-gold project in the Philippines from study to construction? The answer in its disclosures is a financing push: the company has hired a string of financial advisers, refreshed its management team, won Shareholder approval for a related-party convertible note and is talking to lenders and strategic partners. It has also stressed that no specific transaction has been agreed.
The company's shares are listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange under the code SAU and trade over the counter in the United States as RTLGF. Research found no S&P Dow Jones Indices announcement, constituent record or company statement placing the stock in the S&P/TSX Composite Index, the S&P/TSX SmallCap index or any other S&P/TSX benchmark.
The Kingking project in brief
Kingking sits in Davao de Oro province on the island of Mindanao. The company describes it as one of the largest undeveloped copper-gold deposits in the world, and it has been declared a project of national significance under Philippine Executive Order No. 79. Company releases also say the government ranks it among its top three priority Mining projects.
A pre-feasibility study released on 31 July 2025 sets out the current development case. It outlines an open-pit operation processing about 100,000 tonnes a day over a 38-year life, based on proven and Probable Reserves of roughly 960 million tonnes. Of that, 849 million tonnes are milling reserves grading 0.26 per cent copper and 0.36 grams per tonne gold, with a further 111 million tonnes of leach material at 0.23 per cent copper. Life-of-mine output is estimated at 4.4 billion pounds of copper and 6.9 million ounces of gold, with the first five years averaging about 129,000 tonnes of copper and 333,000 ounces of gold a year.
What the study numbers do and do not show
At a copper price of US$4.30 a pound and gold at US$2,150 an ounce, the study estimated an after-tax net present value of US$4.18 billion at a 7 per cent discount rate, an after-tax internal rate of return of 34.2 per cent and a payback of 1.9 years. Initial Capital Expenditure was put at US$2.37 billion. Cash costs were estimated at US$2.06 per pound of copper-equivalent, or US$0.32 per pound of copper after gold credits.
These are study-level estimates rather than results, and pre-feasibility work carries wider cost and schedule uncertainty than a definitive feasibility study. The company has said the project is essentially shovel ready, with approvals substantially complete, although its Mineral Processing Permit requires renewal. In November 2025 it said first concentrate production was targeted for 2030. That timetable depends on completing a definitive study and arranging finance, neither of which has been announced as complete.
A year of advisers and management changes
On 24 November 2025, St. Augustine appointed BMO Capital Markets and Macquarie Capital as financial advisers for Kingking. On 14 April 2026, it said it continued to engage with public and private financial institutions, strategic counterparties and other potential capital providers, including funding approaches typically associated with large mining projects and work that could support a definitive feasibility study.
In May 2026, director Nicolaos Paraskevas resigned from the board but stayed on as a consultant on Kingking financing. The company appointed Cecille Marie Bernardo, a certified public accountant, as chief financial officer; James Timothy Armstrong, a mining engineer with 37 years of experience, as chief development officer to help complete the definitive study; and Raymond Ricafort as head of investor relations. On 19 June 2026, it added Singapore-based ELD SG and Eldorado Partners as financial advisers to evaluate financing structures and strategic options.
Capital structure, filings and dividends
At the annual meeting on 26 June 2026, all seven director nominees were elected and shareholders approved an amended option plan. Disinterested shareholders also backed a convertible note financing with TVI Resource Development Phils., Inc., a related party, with about 99.86 per cent support. The company said the note remained subject to Toronto Stock Exchange and final board approvals. The amount and terms were not stated in the meeting results release reviewed for this article.
The share base is large. Exchange data published with the June releases showed 1,579,549,129 shares in issue, a closing price of C$0.185 on 29 June and a Market Value of about C$292 million. Part of that share count stems from July 2025, when Nationwide Development Corporation and 16 arm's-length assignees converted the full principal of a convertible note into 185 million shares.
St. Augustine does not pay a dividend, and no trailing or declared distribution was found, which matches the zero Yield in the source data. Its audited statements for the year ended 31 December 2025 were filed on 1 April 2026, two days after the company warned they would be late because of additional audit work on certain financial instruments and applied for a management cease trade order. Detailed cash, liabilities and loss figures from those statements and later interim reports were not reviewed during this research, so they are not quoted here.
Copper market backdrop
Kingking's appeal rests heavily on copper. Electrification and grid Investment are widely cited as long-term Demand drivers, while new Supply has been slow to arrive. Gold credits add a second Revenue stream. However, metal prices move, and the study's sensitivity to copper and gold assumptions means a downturn would affect both project Economics and the willingness of financiers to commit.
Key risks and milestones
The dominant risk is financing. Raising more than US$2 billion for a single asset typically involves a mix of project debt, offtake or streaming arrangements, strategic Equity and possibly a partner, any of which could dilute existing shareholders or reduce their economic interest. Other risks include permit renewal, community and environmental matters, cost inflation, the jurisdiction, related-party dealings and governance, given the recent late filing.
Milestones to watch are confirmation of the TVI convertible note terms and approvals, any announced financing or strategic partnership, progress towards a definitive feasibility study, and renewal of the Mineral Processing Permit. Until those arrive, the investment case rests on a sizeable study-stage resource rather than on committed funding.

Brent crude oil prices rose above $101 a barrel on Wednesday as an approaching storm threatened oil and gas production in the US Gulf of Mexico, and renewed Houthi attacks in the region added to supply concerns.
International benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery increased 0.9% to $101.50 per barrel at 10.03 a.m. local time (0703 GMT), up from $100.58 at the previous close.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures for November delivery rose 0.8% to $90.12 per barrel from $89.44.
A storm that formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday is moving rapidly toward Louisiana and Mississippi and is expected to become the first hurricane of this year's Atlantic hurricane season within two days, US weather forecasters said.
The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said early Wednesday that the system was expected to reach tropical-storm strength.
Offshore oil fields in the Gulf of Mexico along the storm's projected path account for about 15% of US crude oil production and 5% of natural gas output.
Six refineries operated by Shell, Valero Energy, Marathon, PBF Energy and Chevron could also be affected as the storm approaches the US Gulf Coast, according to reports.
Refineries in US Gulf Coast states account for roughly half of the country's total refining capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day.
The storm is forecast to pass through offshore areas hosting oil and gas production facilities as well as coastal areas with major refineries.

articles.title: Brent Oil Surpasses $101 Amid Saudi Attacks and US Storm Heightening Supply Concerns - Observer Voice
articles.summary: Brent Oil Surpasses $101 Amid Saudi Attacks and US Storm Heightening Supply Concerns  Observer Voice
articles.full_text:
Oil prices surged on Wednesday, with Brent crude surpassing the $101-per-barrel mark. The increase of over 1% was driven by fresh supply concerns that overshadowed optimism from rising crude supplies in the Middle East. Brent crude rose 1.02% to $101.60, while WTI crude climbed 1.05% to $90.38 amid worries about potential disruptions in Saudi Arabia and the US oil sector.
Supply Concerns Amid Rising Middle East Production
Recent forecasts from the US indicate that a storm developing in the Gulf of Mexico could become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days. This storm poses a risk to oil and gas facilities, affecting areas that account for 15% of US crude production and 5% of natural gas production. Six refineries in the storm’s path, located in Gulf states, represent about 50% of the US’s total refining capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day.
Despite the looming storm, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman reported an increase in oil supplies, with the East-West pipeline reaching 5.8 million barrels a day. Additionally, the head of Vitol stated that approximately 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million barrels per day of refined products had been shipped from the Middle East in the past week.
Mixed US Inventory Data
US inventory data presents a mixed picture for the oil market. Sources cited by Reuters indicate that crude and gasoline inventories fell last week, while distillate stocks saw a slight increase. Specifically, US crude inventories decreased by 2.09 million barrels for the week ending October 2.
Tensions in the Middle East have further complicated the supply landscape. The Saudi aviation authority reported that airports in Jazan and Najran were attacked twice on Monday evening amid escalating hostilities with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. These attacks coincide with a major offensive by Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces to reclaim territory lost to the Houthis.
Analysts Predict Continued Price Pressure
Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney, noted that ongoing attacks and refinery outages are likely to sustain elevated oil prices. He stated, “Attacks and refinery outages are likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to crude. Prices will stay elevated near a $100 level without any material de-escalation emerging.”
The broader geopolitical tensions involving Iran remain unresolved. US President Donald Trump expressed uncertainty regarding Iran’s leadership amid ongoing conflicts, stating, “Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country.” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman countered that the US is well aware of Iran’s decision-making structure.

articles.title: Vancouver and Surrey mayors welcome Pacific Link pipeline, while Delta mayor seeks a planning role - Daily Hive
articles.summary: Vancouver and Surrey mayors welcome Pacific Link pipeline, while Delta mayor seeks a planning role  Daily Hive
articles.full_text:
Ahead of the civic election on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, Vancouver mayor Ken Sim has ruled out a municipal legal fight against the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline by the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada, while Surrey mayor Brenda Locke has voiced strong support for the project. Delta mayor George Harvie wants his city to be involved in planning the pipeline and addressing its local impacts.
All three mayors welcomed the prospect of investment and jobs in separate statements issued over the past week, after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced his decision to designate the brand-new oil pipeline as a project of national interest.
Harvie’s approach centres on the pipeline’s proposed endpoint at Roberts Bank in Tsawwassen — in the southwest corner of Delta. The pipeline would extend from the Edmonton area, largely following the existing Trans Mountain pipeline corridor until it reaches the eastern areas of the Lower Mainland.
The project could include a major marine export terminal at Roberts Bank, with a new man-made causeway peninsula adding to the two existing causeways serving BC Ferries’ Tsawwassen terminal and the GCT Deltaport/Westshore terminals. The pipeline could also pass through Delta to reach the new export terminal.
Harvie, who is running for re-election under his Achieving For Delta party, is seeking an active role in planning for Pacific Link and Vancouver Fraser Port Authority’s separate brand-new Roberts Bank Terminal 2 container facility, which would be achieved as a major extension of the existing causeway that supports the GCT Deltaport/Westshore terminals.
He says the City of Delta needs to examine how both the pipeline and new container terminal project could affect residents and businesses when their impacts are combined together.
“These projects represent significant economic opportunities for Delta and for Canada. Our responsibility is to make sure Delta has a seat at the table and that we understand both the benefits and the potential negative impacts for our community,” said Harvie.
The concern extends beyond the pipeline itself. Harvie pointed to potential changes in truck and train traffic from port and industrial growth, as well as greater demands on roads, public transit, and public services, and pressure on farmland and the environment.
He said these effects need to be considered alongside the jobs and business opportunities the investments could bring.
“Major projects are usually planned and evaluated individually, but Delta experiences their impacts collectively,” said Harvie.
Pacific Link is proposed to carry an additional one million barrels of Albertan oil a day to the West Coast for export, with the federal government emphasizing the need to expand access to Asian markets as a way to reduce Canada’s current reliance on the United States.
Carney’s national interest designation places the pipeline project into a single federal review process. The federal government is aiming to finalize the conditions needed to proceed by September 2027, while the proponents work on detailed route planning, environmental studies, cost estimates, public and Indigenous consultations, and other preparations.
Tsawwassen First Nation has also said it wants to be directly consulted on the project, given the potential impacts of the pipeline and export terminal on its lands in the immediate area.
Roberts Bank Terminal 2 would add a new three-berth container terminal in Delta. The federal government has referred it to the Major Projects Office as part of a broader effort to significantly expand the Port of Vancouver’s capacity and improve Canada’s trade connections.
Harvie said he would seek input from Delta residents and businesses as the projects advance, and draw on his experience dealing with federal and provincial ministers to advocate for the community.
He also acknowledged that Delta’s municipal government cannot dictate every decision made by senior governments, other local and regional governments, or project proponents, but asserted Delta’s municipal government needs to participate in those discussions and advocate for measures that address local concerns. He emphasized that such an approach is not anti-development.
“Delta welcomes investment, good jobs, better transportation and responsible economic development,” continued Harvie.
Mayor Sim said his ABC Vancouver party supports projects that expand Canada’s access to overseas markets, attract investment, and reduce its reliance on any single trading partner.
He described the pipeline as a federal matter and said Vancouver’s municipal government would not try to block it under his and ABC’s leadership — partly because the pipeline would not pass through Vancouver’s municipal boundaries.
The mayor also ruled out hiring outside lawyers to challenge the project, arguing that Vancouver should direct its attention to local infrastructure.
“We support a Canada that sells to the world, not one that waits for permission. And being a gateway city sometimes means getting out of the way. As long as I’m Mayor of this city, I have no intention of launching frivolous lawsuits against companies or the federal government who are creating jobs and economic opportunities in Canada,” said Sim.
“I have no intention of using City lawyers or high-priced law firms to try to block a pipeline that doesn’t even touch Vancouver city limits.”
Sim’s comments appear to allude to the very high-profile municipal battles over the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion during the 2010s. His position marks a sharp departure from the approach taken by then-Vancouver mayor Gregor Robertson of Vision Vancouver and then-Burnaby mayor Derek Corrigan of Burnaby Citizens Association, whose municipal administrations pursued legal challenges in their opposition to the project.
The expansion was expected to increase tanker visits at Westridge Marine Terminal on Burrard Inlet from about five per month to about one per day. At the time, Robertson warned that a spill could damage Stanley Park and beaches, while Corrigan warned of harm to tourism and the economy.
Vancouver’s municipal government spend at least hundreds of thousands of dollars on expert advice and public communications. City records released in 2017 note that roughly $400,000 was spent in the preceding years. The City of Vancouver also asked the courts to review the provincial government’s environmental approval of the expansion. Robertson is currently the federal Minister of Housing and Infrastructure for Carney’s administration.
Burnaby’s municipal government reported $1.12 million in legal spending between 2014 and 2018, financed through its share of provincial casino revenue. Its disputes included a fight over municipal authority, with the federal government enabling the Trans Mountain project to proceed with certain terminal work without obtaining approvals required under some Burnaby bylaws, including permits for tree cutting.
Former Vancouver mayor Kennedy Stewart also strongly opposed the Trans Mountain expansion. As the federal NDP MP for Burnaby South, prior to becoming the mayor of Vancouver, he was arrested at a pipeline protest in 2018 and later pleaded guilty to criminal contempt of court. He continued opposing the project as mayor, arguing that it went against climate action and First Nations reconciliation.
After much controversy and delay, the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion reached completion in 2024.
Incumbent Surrey mayor Brenda Locke of the Surrey Connect party also expressed strong support for Pacific Link. Depending on the pipeline’s final route, Pacific Link could pass through parts of Surrey on its way to Roberts Bank in Tsawwassen.
“Prime Minister Carney’s decision to advance Pacific Link is an important step toward diversifying Canada’s energy exports, creating good jobs, and reducing our reliance on any one trade partner,” said Locke in a statement to Indo-Canadian Voice.
“This project, with meaningful Indigenous ownership and a focus on Canadian workers and materials, strengthens our economic sovereignty. Surrey Connect supports nation-building infrastructure that expands markets, generates revenue, and builds long-term prosperity for communities across British Columbia and Canada.”
Locke linked her support for the pipeline to a broader push to strengthen Surrey’s economy, including diesel tax relief for truckers.
“Surrey’s strength has always been its people and its ability to get things done. Supporting our truckers with diesel tax relief and backing projects like Pacific Link are clear ways to protect jobs, strengthen our economy, and position Surrey and Canada for success in a changing global environment,” she added.

Sustainability, resilience, and security constitute formative pillars of the global energy transition. Given that carbon-intensive fossil fuels yield negative environmental repercussions and face depletion in the long term, hydrogen presents a viable solution to accelerate industrial decarbonisation. Industry accounts for over 21 percent of direct global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, with iron, steel, cement, and chemical sectors comprising 71 percent.[1] Hydrogen’s appeal stems from its versatility as an energy carrier, applicability across multiple end-use segments, and ability to be produced from various sources such as water, fossil fuels, and biomass. These factors underscore its potential as a transitional and clean energy tool.[2]
Hydrogen can fuel power generation and serve as energy storage for renewables. It can also be chemically converted into derivatives, including ammonia and methane, which can be leveraged as feedstock for hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, cement, fertilisers, and chemicals. Compared to other renewables, hydrogen is stable, reliable, and capable of meeting high-temperature requirements to decarbonise such sectors.[3]
Figure 1: Hydrogen Applications: An Overview
Source: BloombergNEF[4]
Initial global interest in hydrogen can be traced to the 2019 Group of Twenty (G20) Summit in Japan which drew attention to it as a key industrial decarbonisation tool.[5] The coinciding launch of the International Energy Agency's (IEA) flagship The Future of Hydrogen report established hydrogen as integral to energy transition. National hydrogen strategies subsequently increased from a small handful to over 30 hydrogen road maps by 2021.[6],[7],[8]
Subsequently, countries such as Japan and Germany attempted to fuel their hydrogen economies through ambitious targets, but encountered geographical, cost, and supply–demand mismatch constraints. Japan, for example, has implemented generous hydrogen subsidies for application in fuel cell passenger vehicles.[9] However, its supply of clean hydrogen is constrained by its geography, as the country is energy-import dependent and lacks land capacity for renewable energy expansion, which has constrained domestic green hydrogen deployment. Other forms of transport decarbonisation, therefore, remain more inexpensive and effective for Japan. Germany’s Hydrogen Import Strategy quantifies projected demand and outlines clear infrastructure linkages, but the country faces similar challenges with hydrogen cost competitiveness, as global demand has fallen short of early expectations.[10]
Despite early positive signalling, the global deployment of clean hydrogen and its derivatives have faced several interrelated challenges, namely, high production costs, infrastructural setbacks, regulatory fragmentation, and lack of secure demand off-takers. Consequently, current global hydrogen progress has fallen short of early established targets. In 2025, Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BNEF) estimated that hydrogen production would rise to 5.5 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) by 2030, well below the 25 mtpa combined global national targets.[11],[12] BNEF’s projections stem from low industry demand for hydrogen as well as technical and cost barriers inhibiting large-scale production and transport.
The prospect of hydrogen development remains attractive and well-suited to Gulf Cooperation Council countries (GCC), which are actively conducting feasibility studies with the aim of establishing commercial-scale hydrogen infrastructure projects.[13] First, the region seeks to diversify its economies away from fossil fuels. Simultaneously, due to increasing climate-related impacts, it is accelerating its decarbonisation efforts. Second, GCC countries are geographically well-positioned, nestled between two key import markets such as Asia and Europe, and boast abundant solar and wind resources. There is also mounting interest in nuclear energy exploration. Despite limited freshwater access, improvements in desalination technologies could facilitate water consumption for electrolysers. Third, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia, and Oman have made substantial investments exceeding US$69 billion in strengthening hydrogen infrastructure and have established partnerships with counterparts in Europe and Asia.[14] Consequently, hydrogen production costs in the Middle East are projected to decline significantly by 2030 (see Table 1).

However, hydrogen ambitions vary across the six GCC countries, with the sector largely nascent in Qatar, Kuwait, and Bahrain. These early policy ambitions have yet to translate into continuous investments and tangible infrastructural development. Highlights
- Southern Copper (NYSE:SCCO) Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) eased as copper cooled from recent record territory.
- The Americas-focused miner tracked a softer session for metals and mining names.
- Trade chatter and a cautious macro mood framed the pullback in copper-linked stocks.
Copper had been among the standout performers in the commodity arena, repeatedly pressing to fresh highs as supply struggled to keep pace with demand from grids, vehicles and construction. That strength had lifted the entire copper-mining group, and few names benefited as directly as Southern Copper, given the dominance of the red metal in its revenue mix. When the metal stepped back from those records, the miner felt the move immediately.
A Pure-Play Copper Heavyweight
Southern Copper ranks among the most copper-concentrated of the major producers, with the red metal accounting for the lion's share of its output and revenue. The company also produces molybdenum, zinc, silver and other byproducts, but copper is unmistakably the engine. The company controls some of the largest copper reserves in the industry, anchored by long-life assets in Peru and Mexico. Those reserves give it a lengthy runway of production and a cost position that has historically ranked among the more competitive in the sector. That combination of scale and cost discipline is central to how the name is perceived within the mining group.
Operations Across Peru and Mexico
In Peru, its operations include large open-pit mines and associated processing facilities, while in Mexico it runs an extensive network of mines, smelters and refineries. This geographic spread gives the company a diversified operating footprint within the region, though it also exposes it to the local dynamics of each country. Mining in these jurisdictions carries its own set of considerations, from permitting timelines to community relations and the occasional disruption tied to local conditions. Southern Copper has long operated through such challenges, and its ability to keep metal flowing from its core assets is a recurring theme in how the business is assessed. Steady output from its flagship mines underpins the company's standing as a reliable supplier of the red metal.
Expansion Ambitions on the Horizon
Beyond its producing assets, Southern Copper carries a pipeline of expansion projects aimed at lifting output over time. These include brownfield expansions at existing operations and greenfield developments that could add fresh capacity as the copper market tightens. Advancing these projects is a core part of how the company frames its growth over the longer arc of the commodity cycle. Developing new copper capacity is neither quick nor simple, with permitting, community engagement and large capital outlays all part of the equation. Still, in a world increasingly focused on securing copper for electrification, a producer with a credible pipeline of new metal holds a distinctive place. Readers following Metals and Mining Stocks can place this update within its wider category.
Where Southern Copper Sits in the Sector
On days when the metal climbs, Southern Copper tends to be among the strongest movers in the group; when the metal eases, as it did Thursday, the same concentration means the name feels the move with little cushion from other commodities.
Electrification Keeps Copper in the Spotlight
The long-running case for copper rests on electrification. The metal is indispensable to power grids, electric vehicles, renewable generation and the data centers powering the artificial-intelligence buildout. Each of those themes points toward rising copper demand over time, and that structural backdrop has been a key reason the metal pressed to records earlier in the year. Southern Copper is positioned to supply into that demand, with scale and reserves that few rivals can match. The structural story has underpinned enthusiasm for the name even through short-term wobbles in the spot price.
Byproducts and the Revenue Mix
While copper dominates, Southern Copper's byproduct metals play a supporting role in its results. Molybdenum, used to strengthen steel, along with silver and zinc, contribute to the revenue mix and can provide a modest offset when copper softens. The prices of these metals move on their own cycles, adding texture to the company's earnings profile. On days when byproduct metals stay firm while copper eases, the net effect on revenue can be cushioned somewhat. Still, the overwhelming weight of copper ensures that the red metal remains the dominant driver of how the stock trades.
